title: Answerability-Gain Rewards for Evidence-Label-Free GRU-Mem Gating: An Empirical Investigation

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to replace expensive evidence-position labels for training GRU-Mem update/exit gates in recurrent memory agents. No prior paper explicitly addresses this specific objective. While papers like [3] and [10] discuss training memory agents for long-context reasoning, they do not focus on replacing evidence-position labels specifically. Papers such as [6], [9], and [10] address memory agent workflows and optimization strategies but do not target the same problem-class level objective of replacing evidence-position labels.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves using answerability-gain rewards, a dense per-chunk signal measuring the change in answer confidence (teacher-forced log-likelihood of the correct answer) after each memory update, combined with per-step cost penalties for early exit. Paper [6] discusses dense reward signals for memory agents but focuses on sparse reinforcement learning signals and memory buffer updates, which differ substantively from the proposed mechanism. Paper [12] introduces dense rewards derived from task progress estimation, which is conceptually similar to the answerability-gain rewards but does not involve teacher-forced log-likelihood or per-step cost penalties. Paper [13] discusses token-level credit assignment using PPO, but this mechanism is distinct from the proposed answerability-gain rewards. No prior paper contains a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its method on RULER-QA across context lengths from 28K to 224K tokens against outcome-only reward baselines. Papers [6], [7], [9], [10], and [16] all evaluate memory agents for long-context question answering tasks, using benchmarks and metrics that align with the evaluation design of the contribution. For example, [7] systematically evaluates memory-augmented methods on long-context dialogues annotated for question-answering tasks, and [16] evaluates memory agents via incremental multi-turn interactions. These prior works share the same evaluation design, even if the specific benchmark (RULER-QA) differs.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of long-context recurrent memory agents. Papers [3], [6], [9], [10], and [16] all address long-context reasoning and memory agents, which is the same general application area. While the specific sub-problem or dataset may differ, the domain is covered by these prior works.
